original_question: In the attempted derivation of an osp(1|2) triangle sum rule, is it mathematically legitimate to identify coefficients over tensor operators S_c even though some of these operators are proved in the paper to be zero by construction?
target_in_paper: Section 14, Conclusion (p. 26), in the author’s concluding remark about the final step of the osp(1|2) △S-sum-rule derivation: after obtaining the quasi-final identity (12.5), one may ask whether it is really "licit" to identify over tensor operators like S^c, even though some such tensor operators are proved to be zero by construction via Theorems 1 and 2.
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the right part of the paper: it concerns the osp(1|2) sum-rule derivation, the coefficient-identification step over tensor operators S^c (more precisely S^e in Eq. (12.5)), and the possible obstruction created by tensor operators that the paper proves to vanish by construction.
missing_details: The paper’s tensor operators are the iterated osp(1|2) operators S^κ(c0,d0), with c0 and d0 assumed real in the paper; the draft does not name these parameters or the operator family precisely.

The issue arises at a specific stage: Section 12 compares two expressions for the triple product [[S^a × S^b]^c × S^d]^e and obtains the quasi-final △S-sum-rule identity (12.5), where the identification is over the common tensor operator S^e.
The intended object is a genuine osp(1|2) super-triangle sum rule involving △S and 6-j^S symbols, not just a generic 'triangle sum rule' phrased in su(2)-style language.

The vanishing operators are not arbitrary: Theorem 1 states that [S^k × S^{k′}] of rank k+k′−1/2 is zero for all integral k,k′, and Theorem 2 states that [S^k × S^κ] of rank |k−κ|+1/2 is zero for all integral k and half-integral κ.
The draft does not specify the quantifiers on the indices a,b,c,d,e,f or the integral/half-integral parity structure that is essential in Sections 12 and 13.

The f-summation in the right-hand side analysis is osp(1|2)-specific: in Section 13 it may run with step 1/2 and split into integral and half-integral sectors; this matters for the form of the identification problem.

The paper’s larger obstruction is not only identification over S^e; after that, one still has to perform the 'ultimate identification' over the two independent parameters c0+d0^2 and d0^2 through binomials (c0+d0^2)^(Ω−m)(d0^2)^m.

Section 13 introduces homogeneous polynomials R^Ω and R^{Ω_f} of degrees Ω and Ω_f, built from products of the P^ω-polynomials and their expansion coefficients x; the draft omits this homogeneity and degree data.

Conjecture 1 is nearby context: the coefficients x_m^π(λ,κ) in the P^π-expansions are conjectured to be integers, and this unresolved polynomial structure is part of why the final identification remains open.
The author explicitly says this licitness question is 'certainly not the most important aspect'; the main declared open problem is still the analytical completion of the osp(1|2) △S-sum rule.

There is no nilpotency condition or 'for all sufficiently large m' clause in this paper; the relevant vanishing is structural zero-product behavior from Theorems 1 and 2, not eventual coefficient vanishing.
refined_question: For the iterated osp(1|2) tensor operators S^κ(c0,d0) with c0,d0 ∈ ℝ used in the paper, and at the specific stage where the two recoupled expressions for [[S^a × S^b]^c × S^d]^e lead to the quasi-final identity (12.5), is it mathematically legitimate to identify the coefficients of the common tensor operator S^e term-by-term in order to obtain a genuine △S-sum rule for 6-j^S symbols, despite the fact that the same paper proves the existence of nontrivial zero tensor operators by construction—namely the families given in Theorem 1 for integral k,k′ and in Theorem 2 for integral k and half-integral κ?
justification: Your draft is tracking a real remark in the paper, but not one of its numbered conjectures: in the Conclusion the author explicitly asks whether it is really "licit" to identify over tensor operators like S^c, precisely because some tensor operators are proved zero by construction. The nearby mathematical setup is Eq. (12.5) in Section 12, where the comparison of two expressions for a triple product produces a quasi-final △S-sum-rule identity over S^e, and Sections 13-14 explain that the deeper unresolved obstacle is the subsequent polynomial identification over the two independent real parameters c0+d0^2 and d0^2. So the sharpest paper-faithful rewrite keeps the licitness issue, anchors it to Eq. (12.5), and names the two zero-product theorems whose existence motivates the concern, without broadening the question into the entire open problem of solving for all x-coefficients.
